bug_semantics: The MCP-exposed ado installer accepted an attacker-controlled package name and interpolated it into executable Stata source without validation or quoting. A package containing a newline therefore terminated the intended `ssc install` command and introduced another Stata command; Stata's `shell`/`!` escape then executed an arbitrary OS command with the server process's privileges. In the advisory-era implementation, `ado_package_install` forwarded `package` through `SSC_Install.install()` to `StataController.run()`/`pexpect.sendline()`; in the original implementation, the same untrusted value was written into a `.do` file and that file was executed by Stata.
flaw_origin: b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607 first added the MCP tool `ssc_install(command, is_replace)` in `src/stata_mcp/__init__.py`: lines 646-650 interpolated `command` directly into `write_dofile(f"ssc install {command}...")` and immediately passed the resulting file to `stata_do`. The immediate parent had no SSC-install tool or SSC command construction. Later commits moved the server code and replaced this implementation with the `ado_package_install(package)`/`SSC_Install.install(package)` framework, preserving the same missing trust-boundary validation rather than originating it.
ai_marker: absent: `git cat-file -p b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607` shows author and committer `SongTan <sepinetam@gmail.com>` and the message `refactor: rename StataController and StataDo directories to snake_case naming convention`; the commit object has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, bot identity, or other AI trailer/marker.
evidence: First-party advisory https://github.com/SepineTam/mcp-for-stata/security/advisories/GHSA-49m4-vp58-wgc9 identifies `src/stata_mcp/stata/builtin_tools/ado_install/ssc_install.py` package interpolation, delivery to Stata, newline command injection, and the patched boundary 1.19.0; the release reference is https://github.com/SepineTam/mcp-for-stata/releases/tag/v1.19.0.

`git log --all --reverse -S'ssc install {command}' -- '*.py'` led to b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607. Its patch adds the complete `ssc_install` MCP tool. At that tree, `src/stata_mcp/__init__.py:630-650` exposes attacker-controlled `command`, interpolates it into `ssc install` source, writes the source to a do-file, and calls `stata_do`; lines 690-699 construct `StataDo` and execute that file.

Direct parent verification: `git grep -n -E 'ssc_install|ssc install \{|ssc install' 9ef0a4076b51955786a29afc7de4bb1c782b6faf -- src` returned no matches. Thus neither the vulnerable MCP entry point nor its SSC command construction exists in the immediate parent tree.

History continuity: 51e4bf3aff9e188de931ae77686bd42bc77524da only extracted the MCP server from `src/stata_mcp/__init__.py` to `src/stata_mcp/mcp_servers.py`; 0001cec1135824bc77dca6fe116ac6b06a2c8c4d introduced the unsanitized `SSC_Install.install()` framework implementation; and 28e0757d5d0df5a9c6be257218e277dff332659e renamed the tool to `ado_package_install`, changed `command` to `package`, and routed it through `SSC_Install`. These preserve/refactor the flaw first introduced by b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607, so none is the BIC.

Last-vulnerable-tree check: at tag v1.18.2, `src/stata_mcp/stata/builtin_tools/ado_install/ssc_install.py` still constructs `install_command = f"ssc install {package}{self.REPLACE_MESSAGE}"` and runs it without validation. `src/stata_mcp/mcp_servers.py:626-632` registers `ado_package_install` in profile `all`, while `src/stata_mcp/cli/_handlers.py:298-300` defaults the profile to `all`.

Direct remediation: b2bc49ec447836e0b1d442ece472c42b7f78724b adds `src/stata_mcp/guard/input_validation.py`, makes SSC/net package names pass a strict identifier validator, and calls `validate_ado_package_name(package, source="ssc")` before constructing the Stata command. Its added tests explicitly reject a newline-bearing `regress\nshell` value. Follow-on hardening 1641e93a71e7d1600adb2c7ab1041370d43347d4 and 7a00a338f0efd2c9b186a3923e6b56d8828db804 retained validation and added confirmation/policy changes, but b2bc49ec447836e0b1d442ece472c42b7f78724b is the first direct fix for this injection.

Version-boundary ancestry: `git merge-base --is-ancestor b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607 v1.7.0` succeeds while the same check against v1.6.3 fails, locating the first affected tagged release at v1.7.0. The BIC remains present through v1.18.2. `git merge-base --is-ancestor b2bc49ec447836e0b1d442ece472c42b7f78724b v1.18.2` fails and the check against v1.19.0 succeeds; v1.19.0 calls the package validator before interpolation and allows only ASCII alphanumerics for SSC/net package names. This confirms the advisory's 1.19.0 patched boundary (while tags before v1.7.0 predate the feature despite the advisory's broad `< 1.19.0` range).

BIC-only attribution: the raw b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607 commit object names human author/committer SongTan and contains no trailers after its one-line message. No evidence from later commits, branches, PR text, or the fix was used for attribution.
reasoning: The causal lifecycle starts at b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607, not at the later file/class additions highlighted by the advisory. That commit created the first externally callable SSC installer and crossed the trust boundary incorrectly by embedding the tool argument directly in executable Stata text. A newline changes the generated program from one intended install command into multiple commands, and Stata's shell escape turns the injected line into OS execution. The parent-tree grep establishes immediate-parent absence. Subsequent extraction, renaming, and framework commits changed file paths, parameter names, and the delivery mechanism but carried forward the same unvalidated interpolation; treating one of those refactors as the BIC would miss the true origin. Tag ancestry places introduction between v1.6.3 and v1.7.0, preserves it through v1.18.2, and places the first validation fix b2bc49ec447836e0b1d442ece472c42b7f78724b in v1.19.0. The BIC is an ordinary single-parent commit with preserved history, so there is no squash to decompose. Finally, the BIC commit object has only a human author/committer and no AI marker, which requires NOT_AI under the BIC-only rule.
